etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English hound, from Old English hund, from Proto-West Germanic *hund, from Proto-Germanic *hundaz. Cognate with West Frisian hûn, Dutch hond, Luxembourgish Hond, German Hund, German Low German Hund, Danish hund, Faroese hundur, Icelandic hundur, Norwegian Bokmål hund, Norwegian Nynorsk hund, and Swedish hund, from pre-Germanic *ḱuntós (compare Latvian sùnt-ene (“big dog”), enlargement of Proto-Indo-European *ḱwṓ (“dog”) (compare Old Irish cú (“dog”), Tocharian B ku, Lithuanian šuõ, Armenian շուն (šun), Russian сука (suka)). Doublet of canine.

In 14th-century England, hound was the general word for all domestic canines, and dog referred to a subtype resembling the modern mastiff and bulldog. By the 16th century, dog had become the general word, and hound had begun to refer only to breeds used for hunting.

definitions.definition: A dog, particularly a breed with a good sense of smell developed for hunting other animals.

quote.citation: 1996, Marc Parent, Turning Stones, Harcourt Brace & Company, →ISBN, page 93:
quote.text: On the way out of the building I was asked for my autograph. If I'd known who the signature hound thought I was, I would've signed appropriately.

quote.citation: 2004, Jodi Picoult, My Sister's Keeper, Simon & Schuster,, →ISBN, page 483:
quote.text: I still do not know if he's taken on this case because he's a glory hound, because he wants the PR, or if he simply wanted to help Anna.

definitions.definition: (by extension) A male who constantly seeks the company of desirable women.

quote.citation: 1915, Norman Duncan, "A Certain Recipient", in Harper's, volume 122, number 787, December 1915, republished in Harper's Monthly Magazine, volume 122, December 1915 to May 1916, page 108,
quote.text:
"Are you alone, Goodson?  […]  I thought, perhaps, that the  […]  young woman, Goodson, who supplanted Mary?" […] 
"She had a good many successors, John."
"You are such a hound, in that respect, Goodson," said Claywell, "and you have always been such a hound, that it astounds me to find you—unaccompanied."

quote.citation: c. 1608–1609 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedy of Coriolanus”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene vi]:
1973, Elizabeth Walter, Come and Get Me and Other Uncanny Invitations:
quote.text: 'You blackmailing hound,' the parrot said distinctly, in what Hodges recognized as General Derby's voice. Anstruther turned pale.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English hounden, from the noun (see above).

quote.citation: 2019 April 11, Marcel Theroux, “Machines Like Me by Ian McEwan review – intelligent mischief”, in The Guardian‎[3]:
quote.text: More pertinently for the plot, another marked difference from history is that the United Kingdom of this 1982 is precociously computerised. Instead of having been hounded to death for his homosexuality, the scientist Alan Turing is thriving and lauded.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To urge on against; to set (dogs) upon in hunting.

quote.citation: 1897, Andrew Lang, The Book of Dreams and Ghosts, page 162:
quote.text: We both thought we saw what had the appearance to be a fox, and hounded the dogs at it, but they would not pursue it.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English hownde, hount, houn, probably from Old Norse húnn, from Proto-Germanic *hūnaz.
